scenes.title: Many books, one shelf
scenes.body: The word Bible comes from a Greek phrase, ta biblia — the books. It was never one dictated volume. It is a library: laws, poems, letters, protest, and stories, written across many centuries by many hands, and only later bound as one.

scenes.title: Law, prophets, writings
scenes.body: Jewish scripture, which Christians call the Old Testament, settled into three shelves. Torah is instruction, Genesis through Deuteronomy. The Prophets run from Joshua through the writing prophets. The Writings hold Psalms, Job, and the rest. Jewish Bibles and most Protestant ones share those Hebrew books. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles also include writings such as Wisdom and Maccabees — the deuterocanon, often called the Apocrypha.

scenes.title: Good news, then mail
scenes.body: The New Testament is shorter and later. Four gospels tell of Jesus as proclamation, not as neutral minutes. Acts follows the first communities. Then letters — most of them older than the written gospels — and one apocalypse, Revelation, in the coded imagery of a pressured people. Twenty-seven books, in the form almost all churches share.

scenes.title: Hebrew, a little Aramaic, then Greek
scenes.body: Most of the older library is Hebrew. Parts of Daniel and Ezra are Aramaic, the everyday language of Jesus. The New Testament comes to us in Greek, the common written tongue of the eastern Roman world. Jesus almost certainly taught in Aramaic. The gospels are already a translation of his voice.

scenes.title: Genre is not a trick
scenes.body: A psalm is not a census. A parable is not a statute. Apocalypse is not a newspaper from the future. Readers get lost when every line is forced into the same kind of claim. These films will keep saying which kind of text you are in — history, confession, or a question the churches still argue.

scenes.title: Memory, then ink
scenes.body: Israel’s stories lived in worship and recitation before any finished book. Scribes gathered them — courts, priests, prophets. Books were edited. That is not a scandal. It is how ancient libraries were made. You can sometimes hear more than one voice in a single scroll.

scenes.title: What the caves can prove
scenes.body: The Dead Sea Scrolls, found near Qumran, show that Jewish communities already copied books we know — Isaiah among them — more than a century before Jesus. They also copied other writings that never became scripture. The caves are a window, not a conspiracy. They do not reveal a secret Bible the church buried.

scenes.title: Use came before the final list
scenes.body: Christians did not vote a New Testament into existence in an afternoon. Communities read some books in worship and set others aside. By the later second century, Irenaeus is defending four gospels, not one blended story and not a dozen. Lists still wobble at the edges for a while.
scenes.note: Hebrews, James, 2 Peter, and Revelation were among the slowest to be shared everywhere.

scenes.title: Three rough pressures
scenes.body: Historians describe pressures more than a checklist. Was a book old, and tied to the apostles or their circle? Was it read widely when churches gathered? Did it fit the faith already prayed — a creating God, a truly human Jesus, one story with Israel rather than a throwaway god of the older scriptures? Marcion, who wanted a Bible cut off from Israel, pushed the church to say no.

scenes.title: This library has always traveled
scenes.body: Jewish scholars in Alexandria made the Septuagint, a Greek version of the scriptures, before Jesus was born. Jerome’s Latin Vulgate shaped the medieval West. Later, translators risked prison to put the text in everyday speech. Translation is not a modern accident. It is how these books have moved.

scenes.title: A small place in a large empire
scenes.body: Galilee was villages, fishing towns, and estates. Rome ruled through client kings. Herod Antipas held Galilee during Jesus’s public life. Nazareth was obscure. The gospels do not apologize for that. They start there.

scenes.title: Tax, Temple, and a prefect
scenes.body: The Temple in Jerusalem was the center of Jewish worship and a political fact. Pontius Pilate, prefect of Judea, is the kind of official Rome used: armed, tax-minded, and remembered by Jewish and Roman writers as harsh. Crucifixion was a Roman penalty, especially for people treated as a threat to order.

scenes.title: Not one waiting room
scenes.body: Many Jews hoped God would set things right. They did not all hope in the same shape. Some looked for a king in David’s line. Some for a purified Temple. Some for God to act with no human king at all. Messiah means anointed one. In this century it was a title with more than one portrait.

scenes.title: What historians will say out loud
scenes.body: The gospels open Jesus’s public life beside John the Baptist, a prophet of repentance whom Antipas later killed. Historians, including many who are not Christian, widely agree on a core: Jesus was a Jewish teacher associated with John, remembered as a healer, who gathered followers and was crucified in Jerusalem under Pilate around the year 30.
scenes.note: The infancy stories in Matthew and Luke do not match scene for scene. They are confession as well as chronicle. The public career is on firmer historical ground than the manger.

scenes.title: Do not mash them together
scenes.body: History can say a great deal about the setting and the public life. The claim that this man is God-with-us, born of Mary, the eternal Son — that is the church’s confession. An honest film keeps the two sentences apart. Both belong in the story. They are not the same kind of claim.

scenes.title: The kingdom is the subject
scenes.body: If you remember one theme, remember kingdom of God. Not a flag, and not a private mood. In the synoptic gospels Jesus speaks as if God’s reign is arriving — close enough to change how you forgive, spend, eat, and see the poor. He rarely defines it. He tells stories.

scenes.title: Stories that do not behave
scenes.body: A sower wastes seed. A father runs toward a shameful son. A Samaritan, the wrong neighbor, stops on the road. Parables are not cute morals pasted on. In the gospels they sort a crowd. They use ordinary Galilean life — soil, coins, weddings — to say something unsettling about God.

scenes.title: Who is allowed to sit
scenes.body: Again and again the gospels put Jesus at table with people respectable teachers avoided: collectors of Roman tax, people labeled sinners. A shared meal was a social map. To eat together said: these people belong in the picture of the kingdom. The later Christian supper is, in part, a memory of those meals.

scenes.title: Pharisees were not a cartoon
scenes.body: The Pharisees were a Jewish renewal movement, serious about the law in ordinary life, and ancestors of later rabbinic Judaism. The gospels show sharp fights with some of them about sabbath, purity, and authority. They also show Pharisees who warn Jesus, and Nicodemus, who stays near. Painting all Jews, or all Pharisees, as villains is a misreading — and a historic source of harm.

scenes.title: A reputation for deeds
scenes.body: The gospels are full of healings and exorcisms, told as signs that the kingdom is breaking in, not as tricks for hire. Historians argue about what happened in any one scene. What they do not need to invent is the reputation: Jesus was remembered as a doer of deeds, and as a teacher whose authority did not come from a school.

scenes.title: The week the city was full
scenes.body: The gospels bring Jesus to Jerusalem at Passover, when pilgrims remembered Israel’s rescue from Egypt. He enters to a welcome, disturbs the Temple courts, and teaches under watch. Temple leadership and the Roman prefect both had reasons to fear a spark. Passover was exactly when sparks were dangerous.

scenes.title: The accounts share a spine
scenes.body: He is arrested at night. Hearings before Jewish leaders and before Pilate do not line up scene for scene. That is normal in ancient narrative, and it is honest to say so. The core is stable across the four gospels, and it matches what Paul already repeats in the 50s: Christ crucified. A Roman execution followed.
scenes.note: John does not stage the night council the way Mark does. The path to Pilate, and then to a cross, is the shared spine.

scenes.title: A public, shameful death
scenes.body: Crucifixion was slow and meant to erase a person. The gospels add a charge posted up — king of the Jews — the kind of mocking title Rome used on a would-be claimant. The texts say his closest followers had run. Christians have always insisted this death was not a mistake the faith later edited out. It is the center.

scenes.title: Buried, then proclaimed
scenes.body: Jesus is buried. Joseph of Arimathea is named. Then the gospels say the tomb was empty and that Jesus met his followers — women first in those narratives, then others. The earliest written summary is not a gospel. It is a short creed Paul quotes in 1 Corinthians 15, already traditional when he writes in the mid-50s, within about twenty-five years of the death.

scenes.title: A crucified messiah was a scandal
scenes.body: Nobody in this world was waiting for a messiah Rome had publicly killed. The usual endings were a new leader, or going home. Instead this movement says the God of Israel raised him, and starts saying so in the same city. Historians can document the announcement, the early creed, and the cost. Whether the tomb was empty is where faith and historical judgment part company — and where Christians say the story turns.

scenes.title: A Jewish movement first
scenes.body: The first communities are Jews in Jerusalem. Acts describes shared meals, prayer in the Temple’s orbit, and a public claim about a crucified man. Whether you read Acts as minutes or as shaped history, the start is not a new god and not the city of Rome. It is Israel, arguing about what God has done.

scenes.title: Gentiles force the question
scenes.body: People who are not Jews begin to join. Must the men be circumcised? Must everyone keep the food laws? Acts 15 tells of a Jerusalem meeting that says no: Gentiles do not have to become Jews first. Paul’s letters, our earliest Christian documents, fight this question in real time. The church’s argument with itself is older than its cathedrals.

scenes.title: Letters before gospels
scenes.body: The letters of Paul are older than Mark, Matthew, Luke, and John. They are not biographies. They are pastoral arguments: what the supper means, how Jews and Gentiles are one body, how to live while you wait. Paul had opposed the movement, then joined it. He writes as a Jew, called, he says, to the nations.
scenes.note: Almost everyone counts Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, and Philemon as his. Letters such as Ephesians and the Pastorals are still debated.

scenes.title: No church buildings yet
scenes.body: For a long time there was no Christian architecture. People gathered in homes and workshops. Baptism marked entry. Bread and cup marked the meal. Leadership was local and uneven. Letters were read aloud — most believers could not study them alone. Faith was spoken and shared before it was a private book.

scenes.title: Persecution was real, and uneven
scenes.body: The empire did not run one three-hundred-year manhunt. Pressure was local, and sometimes fierce: Nero’s cruelty in Rome after the fire of 64, and later wider demands to honor the emperor. Christians could look disloyal because they skipped civic rites. They also grew. By the third century they were a visible network, still illegal on paper, already too many to be a rumor.

scenes.title: One argument, many teachers
scenes.body: The early movement was not one neat denomination. Teachers disagreed about who Jesus was, whether the God of Israel was his Father, and whether the body mattered. Some, later called gnostic, treated the world as a mistake to escape. The emerging mainstream said the opposite: creation is good, Jesus was truly human, and Israel’s scriptures stay.

scenes.title: Constantine changes the weather
scenes.body: In 313 Constantine and Licinius granted toleration, the so-called Edict of Milan. Christianity moves from a risky allegiance to a legal one, and soon to a favored one. That does not make the claims true. It changes everything practical: buildings, money, law, and the temptation to confuse the cross with the sword. Christians have argued about that bargain ever since.

scenes.title: One word, a whole fight
scenes.body: Was the Son of the same being as the Father, or the first and greatest creature? The Council of Nicaea sided with same-being — homoousios — against Arius. Hearts did not all settle overnight. The creed tied to Nicaea, expanded in 381 at Constantinople, is still said in churches of East and West. It is a boundary, not a biography of Galilee.

scenes.title: Fully one, fully the other
scenes.body: Chalcedon tried to say that Jesus is fully God and fully human without blending the two into a third thing. Many churches received that definition. Others did not, and they are still here. Christian history is not a Western line with footnotes. The dissenters are churches, not errors that vanished.
scenes.note: The Oriental Orthodox family includes the Coptic, Armenian, Syriac, Ethiopian, and Eritrean churches.

scenes.title: A fence, not the whole pasture
scenes.body: A creed is short on purpose. It does not retell Galilee, and it does not replace the library. It says: inside this faith, these confusions are not optional. You can learn the Nicene Creed in a minute and still spend a life on the gospels it points back to. Study the decision. You are not being drafted by a film.

films.title: East, West, and the Long Middle

scenes.title: Two lungs
scenes.body: Greek East and Latin West slowly became different Christian cultures: language, liturgy, law, and the role of the pope. In the West, monasteries kept texts, farms, and a pattern of prayer when some cities shrank. This is not a dark age in the sense of nothing happened. It is a long age in which most Christians were not European at all.

scenes.title: Churches that were already old
scenes.body: Ethiopia’s church is ancient. Egypt’s Copts lived on past Chalcedon. Syriac Christians spread through Mesopotamia and into Asia. India holds a tradition of Thomas Christians long before Portuguese ships. Nubia, along the Nile, was Christian for centuries. A film that starts in Canterbury and never leaves has already lost half the map.

scenes.title: A schism with a long fuse
scenes.body: The textbook year is 1054: mutual excommunications between a papal legate and the patriarch of Constantinople. The split was older and younger than that day — custom, politics, and the filioque, a Western addition to the creed meaning “and the Son.” East and West still share baptism, scripture, and the early councils. They do not share one communion.

scenes.title: The crusades, without the costume
scenes.body: Called first as armed pilgrimage, the crusades became wars of religion with theft, massacre, and political greed in the mix — including violence against Jews in Europe and the sack of Christian Constantinople in 1204. They are part of church history. They are not a model. Telling them clearly is part of telling the truth.

scenes.title: Beauty and rot in the same centuries
scenes.body: From the twelfth century, universities and friars — Dominican and Franciscan among them — argued theology in public. Cathedrals were sermons in glass for people who would never own a book. Mystics wrote of prayer. Bought offices and heavy systems of penance were also real. The beauty and the rot grew together. Both show up in what happens next.

scenes.title: A monk and a printing press
scenes.body: Martin Luther, an Augustinian, protested the sale of indulgences and a wider system of merit he could not find in Paul. The ninety-five theses were a scholar’s bid to argue. The press made them a public crisis. He translated scripture into German. He also wrote against Jews in ways later centuries used with cruelty. A learning film does not sand that off.
scenes.note: On the Jews and Their Lies (1543) was quoted long after him. It belongs on his shelf, not in a footnote you skip.

scenes.title: Not one protest
scenes.body: Zwingli and Calvin reshaped cities. The English Reformation mixed conviction with a king’s marriage. Radicals sought believers’ baptism and, sometimes, a new society. Rome answered at the Council of Trent: scripture and tradition, a corrected clergy, new religious orders, art that taught. The Reformation is not a Protestant victory lap or a Catholic collapse. It is a split that made Western Christianity plural.

scenes.title: Conviction with armies
scenes.body: Europe spent generations at war with theology on the banners — peasants’ revolts, the Thirty Years’ War, the hunting of Anabaptists and Huguenots, Catholics under Protestant rulers and the reverse. Doctrine mattered. So did land and dynasty. Conviction is not fake because it was abused. Armed with a state, it devastated neighbors the gospel names.

scenes.title: Mission tangled with empire
scenes.body: From the sixteenth century on, Catholic orders and later Protestant societies carried the faith onto coasts Europe was also conquering and trading. Some missionaries defended indigenous people against colonists. Some baptized conquest. The moral result is mixed, and the numerical result is vast. Christianity did not stay a European possession. In many places it became more local than the empire that ferried it.

scenes.title: The map turns over
scenes.body: Pentecostal worship, rising in poor and mixed congregations in the early 1900s, is now among the largest Christian forces on earth. The Second Vatican Council reset Catholic worship and the reading of scripture. And the demographic center moved. Most Christians today live in Africa, Latin America, and Asia, not in the old capitals of Christendom. The library, the life, and the ages are still being read — by a church that looks less and less like one nation.
